messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 73

# The Weight of What He Saw

Marcus is a 39-year-old construction worker who has spent the better part of his adult life building things — framing houses, pouring foundations, reading blueprints with the casual fluency of someone who has done it for so long it feels like a second language. He is broad-shouldered and quiet in the way that men who work with their hands often are, more comfortable with a nail gun than with conversation. Until two years ago, he would have described himself as someone who handled pressure well. He no longer uses that description.

It happened on a Tuesday morning in late October. Marcus was working a commercial site downtown — a mid-rise renovation project, the kind of job he had done dozens of times. He was on the fourth floor when he heard it: a sound he still cannot fully name, somewhere between a crack and a groan, followed immediately by screaming. A scaffold on the adjacent section of the building had failed. He watched his coworker and friend of eleven years, a man named Danny, fall. He watched everything that followed. He was close enough that it felt, in some terrible way, like participation.

The first weeks afterward, Marcus told himself he was fine. He went back to work after three days because staying home felt worse — the silence of his apartment was its own kind of punishment. But the site had changed for him, or rather, he had changed on it. He began scanning constantly, cataloguing every elevated platform, every load-bearing connection, every piece of equipment overhead. His crew noticed he had become short-tempered, snapping at younger workers over minor safety lapses in ways that felt less like supervision and more like desperation. He couldn't explain it to them. He barely understood it himself.

Sleep became the next thing to go. He would lie down exhausted and find himself back on that fourth floor, watching it happen again, sometimes in slow motion, sometimes faster than it actually was. He would wake at two or three in the morning with his heart slamming against his ribs, the sheets damp, the darkness of his bedroom feeling briefly like the wrong place entirely. He started leaving the television on through the night just to have something to orient himself to when he woke.

Marcus has been divorced for four years — the marriage ended before the accident, for reasons he describes as "the usual ones," meaning long hours, emotional distance, growing apart. He has two children, a boy and a girl, whom he sees on alternating weekends. Since the accident, those weekends have become complicated in ways he struggles to articulate. He loves his kids fiercely, but he finds himself emotionally flat in their presence, going through the motions of fatherhood with a competence that looks, from the outside, like normalcy. His daughter told his ex-wife that "Dad seems far away." He heard this secondhand and it stayed with him for weeks.

He has stopped socializing with his crew after shifts, something he used to do regularly. He avoids the specific block where the accident happened, taking a longer route to a job site nearby. He drinks more than he used to — not catastrophically, he insists, but enough that he notices it, enough that he reaches for a beer the way another man might reach for an aspirin. Alcohol is the only thing that reliably quiets the hypervigilance that hums through him now like a frequency he cannot turn off.

What troubles Marcus most, in the quiet moments when he allows himself to think about it, is not the nightmares or the drinking or even the anger. It is the guilt — the persistent, irrational conviction that he should have done something, that he saw it coming a half-second before it happened, that the half-second was enough and he wasted it. He knows, intellectually, that this is not true. He knows it the way you know something you cannot feel.
